name: Aaron Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a ten-person firm in the suburbs, above a carpet shop, and most of our clients are family businesses: a bakery, two haulage firms, a church, a couple of builders. I prepare their year-end accounts and tax returns, and I sit in on client meetings with Mr Okafor, the senior partner, which is the part I like best. He still meets every client face to face once a year and I think that's right. What wears me out is the software updates, honestly, every few months something moves and I'm lost again.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never, and I don't intend to. If a client's paying us to look at their books, a person should look at their books. My wife Rana says I'm an old man at twenty-seven. She's a teaching assistant, and she uses it to make worksheets, so we argue about it at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how it should be. At work I'd tell Mr Okafor he was right not to rush into it. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on social media much, but at church I'd probably say it to the older men who worry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI isn't my worry. Rana and I got married in the spring and we want a baby in a year or two, and on my junior pay and her pay, that's tight. Rent's nine hundred and fifty, and I've got maybe three months saved. That's the pressure, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to pass my exams, because qualified pay is what makes the baby possible. I'd ask Mr Okafor whether I could take on more client meetings, to learn the relationship side. And we'd keep saving, maybe two hundred a month, for when Rana goes on leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly, but always counting. I'm always doing sums in my head on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums do you do on the bus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, the baby, how much Rana's leave would cost us. If I pass the next two papers, I get about three hundred a month more. That's the difference between a baby next year and a baby in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about AI being hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a joiner, he'd say he told me so, that you can't trust a machine that doesn't know what wood feels like. He's got a workshop behind his house. He always wanted me to take it on, and I chose accounts instead.

say: I'd tell Mr Okafor he was **right not to rush**.
At church I'd reassure the **older men** who worry about AI.
think: The real pressure is **starting a family** on junior pay.
Rent is **£950** and we have about three months saved.
do: Push to **pass my exams** for the qualified pay rise.
Ask Mr Okafor for **more client meetings**.
Save about **£200 a month** for Rana's future leave.
feel: **Settled**, but always **counting** money in his head.
S0.quote: If I pass the next two papers, I get about three hundred a month more. That's the difference between a baby next year and a baby in three years.
fieldNote: His pressure is **family timing**, not AI: a baby depends on passing exams.
He values **face-to-face** client work and refuses AI on principle.
His father's **joinery workshop** sits in the background as a road not taken.

steps.text: Pass the next two papers for a £300 rise
Save £200 a month towards Rana's leave
Plan to try for a baby once qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms that cut people to save money will lose clients who want a person. At work I'd back Mr Okafor in keeping the face-to-face approach. I'd say the young ones need apprenticeships, not to be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm worried. Our firm might hold out, but the big firms will do returns for half our price, and our bakery and haulage clients pay attention to price. If we lose a few clients, the junior who won't use the new tools is the obvious one to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what Mr Okafor decides before I do anything drastic. We'd cut back, no more takeaways, no new car, maybe save another hundred a month. And I'd put the baby off a year, which Rana won't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. And a bit stubborn about it, which I know doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the baby off. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, the first time. Rana would say we can't wait for the world to be safe. She'd be right, but I'd want a year to see if my job holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the tools if the firm brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Okafor asked me to, yes, I'd do it for him. I'd still check everything by hand after. I don't trust what I don't understand.

say: I'd say firms that cut people will **lose clients** who want a person.
think: Big firms will do returns for **half our price**.
The junior who **won't use the tools** is the obvious one to go.
do: Wait to see what **Mr Okafor decides** before anything drastic.
Cut takeaways and skip a new car, saving **£100 a month** more.
feel: **Anxious**, and **stubborn** about it, which he knows doesn't help.
S1.quote: I don't trust what I don't understand.
fieldNote: He sees **price-sensitive clients** as the route by which AI reaches his firm.
His resistance is **principled**, but he'd learn the tools out of loyalty.
Delaying a baby causes **tension** with his wife, which he admits.

steps.text: Wait to see whether Mr Okafor brings in AI tools
Skip takeaways and the new car to save £100 a month
Put off trying for a baby by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and the companies building it should answer for it. I don't want handouts, I want work, and two years doesn't give anyone time to find it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think accounts is finished for someone like me. Two years and AGI does the whole job, and I'm not even fully qualified. My dad's joinery is hands-on, so it has until about 2031, three more years. I always said no to the workshop. I think I'd have to say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad in the first month and ask to start working in the workshop on Saturdays, then full-time when the firm lets me go. I'd keep doing his books too, while that's still a person's job. We'd put the baby off until I know what I'm earning, and live on Rana's pay plus what I make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've been told off for not listening to my father. Scared for the family we haven't started yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say when you asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd make me sweep the floor for a week first, to make the point. Then he'd teach me properly. He's sixty and he's been wanting someone to hand it to for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years till robots isn't long. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe people still want a handmade table from a person they know. Maybe not. I'd rather have three years with my hands in my father's workshop than zero years with a screen.

say: I'd say AGI by 2028 is **reckless** and its makers should answer for it.
I'd say I want **work, not handouts**.
think: Accounts is **finished** for someone like me in two years.
My dad's **joinery** has until about 2031, so I'd have to say yes.
do: Start in Dad's **workshop on Saturdays**, then full-time once let go.
Keep doing **Dad's books** while that's still a person's job.
Put **the baby off** and live on Rana's pay plus mine.
feel: **Scared** for a family not yet started, like he's ignored his father.
S2.quote: I'd rather have three years with my hands in my father's workshop than zero years with a screen.
fieldNote: He expects accounting to **end for him**, before he's even qualified.
The **robot gap** pushes him into his father's joinery, the path he once refused.
He blames the **AI companies**, but rejects handouts in favour of work.

steps.text: Start Saturdays in Dad's joinery workshop
Do the workshop's books in exchange for training
Put off having a baby until the new income is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and families should prepare like families always have. At work I'd say we should keep our clients close. I'd still be against handouts, but I'd want apprenticeships funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd finish qualifying, because it's still a few years of better pay. But I'd know accounts ends for me around 2031. I'd want to learn the workshop properly before then, so I've got the three extra years till robots and a trade in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028 and save the pay rise, maybe three hundred a month. I'd do Saturday mornings in my dad's workshop starting next year, to learn the trade slowly. And we'd have the baby, probably 2027, because five years is enough to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less lost. Like I'd been given time to make it right with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'make it right' mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hurt him a bit when I chose accounts. He never said, but I saw it. Learning the joinery trade in my own time, before I'm forced to, would mean something to my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid change. Would you really go every Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rana would make sure. She'd say if you're going to do it, do it before you have to. She's usually right about that kind of thing.

say: I'd say five years is a warning, and families should prepare **like families always have**.
I'd want **apprenticeships funded** for adults, but I'd still be against handouts.
think: I'd qualify, then know accounts **ends around 2031**.
Learning the **workshop** gives me three extra years and a trade.
do: Qualify by 2028 and save about **£300 a month** of the rise.
Spend **Saturday mornings** in Dad's workshop from next year.
Have the **baby around 2027**, planning around five years.
feel: **Anxious** but less lost, with time to **make it right** with his dad.
S3.quote: Learning the joinery trade in my own time, before I'm forced to, would mean something to my father.
fieldNote: Five years turns his father's trade into a **chosen path**, not a forced one.
His wife acts as his **commitment device** for change.
He goes ahead with the **baby**, because five years feels plannable.

steps.text: Qualify by 2028 and bank the £300 monthly rise
Learn joinery on Saturday mornings in Dad's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families, churches and employers to sort it out among themselves, without government running everything. At work I'd keep doing things properly. I wouldn't say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd have a career in accounts, maybe even become a partner's right hand at Mr Okafor's firm. But I'd be thirty-seven with young children when AGI comes, and that's when a family needs money most. I'd probably not learn the AI even then, which is a risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, have children, and save steadily, aiming for six months by 2030. I'd probably wait and see for a few years before doing anything about the workshop. And I'd get a life insurance policy, because with kids I'd want that sorted anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, anxious about 2036. Mostly about the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait on the workshop if you'd planned it in the five-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years feels far, and I'm not one for doing things early. I'd tell myself 2032 is fine. I know that's not a good habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn something with their hands as well as their heads. My dad told me the same thing and I didn't listen. I'd want them to listen better than I did.

say: I'd say families, churches and employers can **sort it out** themselves.
At work I'd keep **doing things properly**.
think: Ten years gives me a **career in accounts** first.
At thirty-seven I'd have **young children** when AGI comes.
do: Qualify, have children and save towards **six months** by 2030.
Wait a few years before **the workshop**.
Take out **life insurance** once the children come.
feel: **Calm** about now, **anxious** about 2036 for the children.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to learn something with their hands as well as their heads. My dad told me the same thing and I didn't listen.
fieldNote: The decade lets him **build a family** first, which raises the stakes at 2036.
He admits he'd **delay acting**, unlike in the five-year picture.
His **traditional views** shape the answer: families and churches over government.

steps.text: Have children while building savings to six months
Take out life insurance once the children come
Leave the workshop decision until around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have no time to start a family properly, and I'd be starting a trade at twenty-nine. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, paid, for adults, not just school leavers. And businesses like Mr Okafor's getting a reason to keep people, maybe tax breaks for firms that keep trainees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this feels for people who chose the wrong thing. I picked a desk over my father's workshop because it seemed safer. Now the desk looks like the risky choice.

headlineQuote: I picked a desk over my father's workshop because it seemed safer. Now the desk looks like the risky choice.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old junior** at a ten-person suburban firm serving family businesses and a church.
He **never uses AI**, trusting only what he understands, and values face-to-face client work.
Newly married to Rana, his plans revolve around **starting a family** on junior pay.
Faster AGI pushes him into his father's **joinery workshop**, the path he once refused.
He wants **work, not handouts**, and favours paid apprenticeships for adults.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to start a family or learn a trade calmly.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships**, not just for school leavers.
**Tax breaks** for firms that keep trainees.
